title: The Question to Pose After Painful Leadership
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article offers a reframing technique for processing painful leadership experiences. Rather than the standard reflective questions — what did I learn, or what will I do differently — the author proposes a more powerful alternative: how can this experience make me a better leader and person? The piece argues this subtle shift moves the memory from being defined by negative emotion to being defined by a forward-looking commitment. It walks through a short exercise readers can try directly on a real memory, arguing that landing hard on a concrete answer changes how the memory is carried going forward, replacing painful recall with a sense of purpose.
points: Painful leadership experiences never fully disappear, but how they're framed can change their emotional weight.
The standard reflective question — what did I learn — is less powerful than a more identity-focused reframe.
The recommended question is: how can this experience make me a better leader and person?
This reframing turns a memory from painful recall into a forward-looking personal commitment.
The article includes a short, concrete exercise readers can apply to their own painful memories.
quotes: The worst events stay stuck in the back of the mind, ready to move forward for yet another round of agonizing reflection.
But asking a more precise question regarding the negative event can make a world of difference.
How the negative experience can make the leader a better person going forward is not just a learning or insight. It is a commitment.
That commitment redirects the energy surrounding the memory and suggests the experience plays an invaluable role in who the leader wants to be in the future.
Your memory will now revolve around your commitment and not around the negative emotions from the episode.
